Providers transporting patients to non-hospital destinations (e.g., clinics, private residences, or non-licensed facilities).

Businesses with incidental brake work as part of broader repair services – limited exposure.
Shops that offer seasonal services (e.g., winterization, AC repair) – aligns with industry demand cycles.

restrictions.rule: Emergency or contract wrecker/towing services are prohibited.

restrictions.rule: Minimum $500 property damage deductible per claim is required for any car wash exposure.

restrictions.rule: 24-hour operations are generally unacceptable.

restrictions.rule: Incidental wrecker exposure is only acceptable if used in connection with the business's own repair service.

restrictions.rule: Rural exposure is preferred over urban or high-crime areas.

restrictions.rule: Shops must comply with all environmental and hazardous waste regulations.

restrictions.rule: All mechanics and technicians must hold appropriate certifications and licenses as required by state law.

restrictions.why: Reduces risk of theft and vandalism.

restrictions.rule: Shops must not operate or have amusement activities (e.g., go-karts, batting cages) on premises.
restrictions.why: Non-standard exposures increase liability and are outside appetite.

preferred: Bakeries that bake on premises with documented food safety programs such as ServSafe certification in place (ensures food safety compliance).

Bakeries or bagel shops with robust cybersecurity measures for online ordering, including data encryption and regular system updates (protects customer data).
Businesses with strong vendor relationships ensuring consistent ingredient quality and supply (reduces operational disruptions).
Operations with early morning hours and peak sales during breakfast and lunch, reflecting stable, predictable patterns (lower volatility).
Staff trained in food safety and, if serving alcohol, in responsible alcohol service (reduces liability exposures).
Establishments that do not serve alcohol or have appropriate liquor liability coverage if they do (limits liquor-related risks).
Bakeries or bagel shops with regular health inspections and a record of compliance (demonstrates regulatory adherence).

Operations with limited seating or takeout-only models, provided all food safety and sanitation controls are in place.
Bakeries or bagel shops with a liquor license that primarily sell baked goods and have liquor liability coverage and trained staff.
Establishments with a history of adapting product offerings to seasonal demand, demonstrating business resilience.
Businesses with a mix of wholesale and retail sales, provided retail operations meet all safety and regulatory requirements.
Bakeries or bagel shops with shared kitchen spaces, provided all tenants adhere to safety and sanitation protocols.

not_acceptable: Bakeries or bagel shops lacking automatic extinguishing systems over cooking equipment (unacceptable fire exposure).
Establishments without any fire or burglar alarm systems (high risk for fire and theft losses).
Operations without documented food safety programs or ServSafe certification (unacceptable food safety risk).
Businesses with repeated or unresolved health code violations (demonstrates ongoing regulatory non-compliance).
Bakeries or bagel shops that serve alcohol without appropriate liquor liability coverage (unacceptable liquor risk).
Staff serving alcohol without documented responsible service training (increases liability exposure).
Operations using online ordering platforms without data encryption or regular system updates (unacceptable cybersecurity risk).
Establishments with a history of major fire or theft losses in the past three years (unacceptable loss history).
Bakeries or bagel shops that only sell (no baking or cooking) but are misclassified as B or C (classification error).
Businesses sourcing ingredients from unverified or high-risk suppliers (increases contamination and recall risk).
Operations with no separation between food prep and customer areas (increases contamination risk).
Establishments operating outside of regulatory compliance, such as lacking required licenses or inspections.
Bakeries or bagel shops with no plan to address known safety deficiencies (unacceptable risk posture).
Businesses that have been denied or cancelled insurance coverage for fire, liability, or theft in the past.

restrictions.rule: All bakeries and bagel shops must have automatic extinguishing systems over all cooking equipment.

restrictions.rule: Monitored fire and burglar alarm systems are required for all locations.

restrictions.rule: Proper sanitation and refrigeration controls must be maintained at all times.

restrictions.rule: Businesses serving alcohol must have appropriate liquor liability coverage and staff must be trained in responsible alcohol service.
restrictions.why: Mitigates liquor-related liability exposures.

restrictions.rule: Operations using online ordering platforms must implement robust cybersecurity measures, including data encryption and regular system updates.
restrictions.why: Protects customer information and reduces cyber risk.

restrictions.rule: Bakeries or bagel shops without required safety measures (fire suppression, alarms, food safety) are not acceptable.
restrictions.why: Unacceptable risk of loss or regulatory action.

restrictions.rule: Establishments must be classified correctly: baking on premises as B, cooking as C, selling only as A.
restrictions.why: Ensures accurate risk assessment and policy application.

restrictions.rule: Businesses with unresolved or repeated health code violations are not eligible.
restrictions.why: Indicates ongoing non-compliance and elevated risk.

restrictions.rule: Ingredient suppliers must be reputable and verifiable.
restrictions.why: Reduces risk of contamination and product recalls.

preferred: Community banks with fewer than 10 branch locations and a strong record of regulatory compliance, demonstrating robust internal controls.
Credit unions serving local residents and small businesses, with no history of regulatory violations in the past five years.
Institutions with a comprehensive employee training program covering compliance, customer service, and data security.
Banks or credit unions that have implemented multi-factor authentication and encryption for all online banking services.
Establishments with a documented disaster recovery and business continuity plan reviewed annually.
Institutions that conduct regular third-party security audits and promptly address any findings.
Banks or credit unions with a dedicated compliance officer responsible for monitoring regulatory changes and internal adherence.
Locations with secure, monitored vaults and restricted access to sensitive areas, supported by electronic surveillance.
Institutions that offer financial literacy programs or community outreach initiatives as part of their service model.
Banks or credit unions with a clean loss history (no claims or losses exceeding $5,000 in the past three years).
Facilities with up-to-date fire suppression systems and regular maintenance of all safety equipment.

Banks or credit unions that have not experienced any data breaches or cyber incidents in the past five years.
Locations with a formalized incident response plan for both physical and cyber threats.
Institutions with a low staff turnover rate, indicating stable operations and consistent customer service.
acceptable: Smaller community banks or credit unions with a consistent compliance history and no recent regulatory violations.
Institutions with fewer than 50 employees and limited geographic reach (single county or region).
Banks or credit unions that primarily serve individuals and small businesses, with minimal exposure to high-risk commercial lending.
Establishments with a documented loss prevention program and regular staff safety meetings.
Institutions that utilize reputable third-party vendors for core banking software and cybersecurity solutions.
Banks or credit unions with a written policy for handling customer data and privacy, reviewed annually.
Locations with secure cash handling procedures and dual control for vault access.
Institutions that have passed all regulatory examinations in the past three years without significant findings.
Banks or credit unions that provide online banking services with basic security protocols in place.
Facilities with controlled public access and visitor sign-in procedures.

Banks or credit unions with a history of stable financial performance and positive customer feedback.
Establishments that have not been subject to any major lawsuits or legal actions in the past five years.

Banks or credit unions that maintain regular communication with local law enforcement regarding security concerns.
not_acceptable: Any institution with a history of regulatory violations or enforcement actions in the past three years.

Banks, building & loan associations, savings & loan associations, credit unions, credit agencies, stockbrokers, finance companies, investment brokers, or similar financial institutions operating outside the community or local focus.
Any risk that is predominantly bailee, such as those holding property primarily for others.
Establishments involved in storage or sorting of cardboard, paper, or rags as a primary business activity.
Institutions with a history of data breaches, cyber incidents, or failure to implement basic cybersecurity measures.
Banks or credit unions with more than $1 billion in assets or operating in multiple states.
Facilities lacking secure vaults or with inadequate physical security measures.

restrictions.rule: Institutions must have a documented and up-to-date compliance program.

restrictions.rule: No acceptance of risks with unresolved or recent regulatory violations.
restrictions.why: Recent violations indicate ongoing compliance or operational issues.

restrictions.rule: Institutions must not engage in predominantly bailee operations.
restrictions.why: Bailee risks are outside the intended appetite and present unique exposures.

restrictions.rule: No acceptance of institutions involved in storage or sorting of cardboard, paper, or rags.

restrictions.rule: Institutions must have a formal loss prevention and employee safety program.
restrictions.why: Promotes a culture of safety and reduces the likelihood of claims.

restrictions.rule: Barber and/or beauty shops must have forms LS-76 and LS-76A attached to be eligible.

restrictions.rule: All staff performing services must be appropriately licensed and certified per state/local regulations.

restrictions.rule: Salons must not offer medical or invasive cosmetic procedures.

restrictions.rule: Operations must be conducted in commercial spaces, not residential or mixed-use premises.

restrictions.rule: Salons must maintain up-to-date professional liability insurance (BP 08 01 or BP 08 09).

restrictions.rule: Salons must adhere to all applicable health, safety, and sanitation regulations.

Shops that provide ongoing employee training on theft prevention and inventory control procedures.
Businesses located in modern, well-maintained commercial shopping centers with up-to-date fire safety infrastructure.

Operations that do not directly import products for retail sale, sourcing inventory only from domestic wholesalers or distributors.

Businesses with a written fire safety plan and regular fire drills for staff.
Retailers that limit high-value inventory exposure by displaying only a small quantity of each item on the sales floor.
Shops with dedicated inventory managers responsible for loss prevention and compliance.

Shops located in older commercial buildings that meet minimum local fire code requirements.
Retailers with minor, explained inventory shortages that are promptly investigated and resolved.
Businesses that source inventory from domestic suppliers with occasional indirect imports handled by third parties.

Operations with locked display cases for only the most expensive items, while other high-value goods are accessible.

Businesses with basic inventory management systems not fully integrated with point-of-sale.
Shops that conduct fire safety checks annually but lack formal fire drills.

Operations with general employee training that includes some inventory control content.

restrictions.rule: Risks may not directly import products for retail sale.

restrictions.rule: Employee training on theft prevention and inventory control must be provided at least annually.

restrictions.rule: Operations with a history of major unexplained inventory shortages or unresolved fire code violations are ineligible.

business_types.name: Beverage Distributors & Retailers (including Beer, Liquor, Wine)

preferred: Retail furniture stores with less than 10,000 sq ft of showroom space and no on-site woodworking or manufacturing (lower fire and liability risk)

Operations that use only pre-assembled or flat-pack furniture (reduces installation hazards)
Stores with dedicated delivery and installation teams that are employees, not subcontractors (better control over safety and training)
Retailers that do not offer repair or refinishing services (limits exposure to chemicals and fire hazards)
Businesses with written safety protocols for lifting, assembly, and delivery (reduces workplace injuries)
Locations with monitored burglar and fire alarms (improved property protection)
Stores that do not handle antique or high-value specialty furniture (limits theft and breakage exposure)
Retailers that require background checks for all installation staff (reduces theft and liability risk)
Businesses with ADA-compliant showrooms and customer areas (reduces accessibility claims)
Operations that do not offer furniture rental or leasing (limits property damage and contractual liability)
Stores with inventory stored off the floor and away from exits (improves fire safety and egress)
Retailers with a written return and warranty policy (improves customer satisfaction and reduces disputes)
acceptable: Furniture stores with up to 25,000 sq ft of showroom space
Businesses that perform minor on-site assembly but no custom carpentry or woodworking
Retailers offering delivery within a 100-mile radius
Operations with a mix of employee and subcontractor installation teams, provided subcontractors are insured
Stores that sell mattresses and bedding in addition to furniture
Retailers with a history of minor, resolved claims (no open or severe losses)
Businesses that occasionally handle commercial installations (offices, hotels, restaurants)
Stores that offer basic repair services (e.g., tightening, minor upholstery fixes) but no refinishing
Operations that use third-party logistics for delivery, with contracts in place
Retailers that display outdoor furniture but do not install permanent outdoor structures
Businesses with seasonal sales fluctuations (e.g., peak during holidays or back-to-school)
Stores located in mixed-use retail centers
Retailers that participate in home shows or trade expos
not_acceptable: Furniture stores with on-site manufacturing, woodworking, or refinishing operations (high fire and injury risk)
Businesses that import and sell untested or uncertified furniture (potential safety and regulatory violations)
Operations that offer structural installations (e.g., built-in cabinetry, wall removal, or electrical work)
Retailers that rent or lease furniture for events or staging (high property damage and theft risk)
Stores that sell or install medical or mobility furniture (e.g., hospital beds, lifts)
Businesses with a history of severe or unresolved claims in the past 5 years
Operations that use only subcontractors for installation without verifying insurance or training
Retailers that store inventory in unprotected warehouses or non-sprinklered buildings
Businesses that offer moving or relocation services in addition to furniture sales
Stores that sell or install playground, gym, or recreational equipment
Retailers that handle antique, rare, or high-value collectible furniture as a primary business
Operations that perform installations in hazardous or industrial environments
Businesses located in areas with high crime rates and no security measures
Stores that do not comply with local zoning, fire, or accessibility regulations
Retailers with no written policies for returns, warranties, or customer complaints

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses with on-site woodworking, manufacturing, or refinishing operations.

restrictions.rule: All installation subcontractors must provide proof of insurance and training.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses that offer furniture rental or leasing services.
restrictions.why: Rental operations have higher property damage and theft risk.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for stores that sell or install medical, mobility, or playground equipment.

restrictions.rule: Inventory must be stored in sprinklered, secured, and monitored facilities.
restrictions.why: Prevents large property losses from fire or theft.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses with unresolved or severe claims in the past 5 years.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses that do not comply with local zoning, fire, or accessibility regulations.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for operations performing structural installations or modifications.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses located in high-crime areas without adequate security systems.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses primarily selling antique, rare, or high-value collectible furniture.

preferred: Garden and landscaping businesses with a primary focus on residential maintenance contracts (due to predictable, lower-risk operations).
Firms offering design, planting, and routine lawn care services without heavy equipment use (minimizes property and liability exposures).
Operations with incidental tree trimming and removal, not as a core service (reduces risk of severe injury/property damage).
Businesses with established relationships with licensed nurseries and reputable material suppliers (ensures quality and reliability).
Companies that do not apply pesticides or herbicides, or only do so on an incidental basis with proper certification (limits pollution and regulatory risk).
Landscaping services with less than $500,000 in business personal property and a monitored central alarm system (reduces theft and fire risk).
Firms with documented safety training and equipment maintenance programs (improves loss control).
Businesses that do not subcontract major portions of their work (better control over operations and liability).
Operations with no history of environmental violations or chemical spills (demonstrates regulatory compliance).
Landscaping companies that do not perform snow removal or only do so on a limited, incidental basis (avoids increased slip-and-fall exposures).
Businesses with written contracts and clear scope of work for all projects (reduces disputes and liability).
acceptable: Garden and landscaping services offering both residential and commercial work, provided tree trimming and removal are incidental.
Firms that apply pesticides or herbicides on an incidental basis and hold all required state/local certifications.
Businesses with seasonal labor, provided all workers are properly trained and supervised.
Operations that perform hardscaping (e.g., patios, walkways) as part of broader landscaping projects.
Companies with up to $500,000 in contents, provided a central alarm system is in place.
Landscaping services that occasionally perform snow removal, but not as a primary business activity.
Firms that rent specialized equipment for large projects, provided proper operator training is documented.
Businesses that maintain general liability coverage and, if offering design services, have professional liability coverage in effect.
Operations that perform minor irrigation system installation or repair as part of landscaping services.
Companies that use approved fertilizers and chemicals, following all environmental regulations.
Firms that provide landscape consulting or design services without direct construction or installation.
Businesses that maintain proper documentation for all pesticide/herbicide applications.
Landscaping services that occasionally subcontract specialized tasks, with certificates of insurance from all subcontractors.
Operations that maintain outdoor property such as fences, provided coverage is specifically endorsed.
Companies that perform maintenance for small commercial properties (e.g., office parks, retail centers) with no large-scale municipal contracts.
not_acceptable: Large maintenance contractors whose primary business is municipal or institutional groundskeeping (exceeds risk appetite).
Businesses where tree trimming or removal is a core service or represents more than 25% of operations (high severity exposure).
Firms that apply pesticides or herbicides as a primary service or without proper certification (unacceptable pollution and regulatory risk).
Landscaping companies with more than $500,000 in business personal property and no central alarm system (increased theft/fire risk).
Operations performing snow removal as a primary business activity (unacceptable slip-and-fall exposure).
Businesses with a history of environmental violations, chemical spills, or regulatory fines (demonstrates poor risk management).
Firms that subcontract the majority of their work without adequate oversight or insurance verification (unacceptable liability exposure).
Companies offering services customary to medi-spas, such as cosmetic treatments or wellness therapies (outside appetite).
Businesses providing drone photography or aerial surveying as part of landscaping services (excluded due to aviation risk).
Operations that include land, water, growing crops, or lawns as covered property, except for vegetated roofs (not insurable property types).
Firms without general liability or professional liability coverage in effect (unacceptable risk transfer).
Landscaping services that operate as schools or training centers (not within appetite).
Businesses that provide tattooing, spa, or massage services (excluded classes).
Firms with tenant exposures that have not been evaluated for general liability or pollution potential.
Companies that do not comply with all applicable licensing, certification, or insurance requirements.

restrictions.rule: Tree trimming and removal must be incidental to primary landscaping services.
restrictions.why: Core tree work presents higher severity risks not contemplated in standard appetite.

restrictions.rule: Pesticide and herbicide application must be incidental and properly certified.
restrictions.why: Primary chemical application increases pollution and regulatory exposure.

restrictions.rule: Large maintenance contractors (municipal/institutional focus) are prohibited.
restrictions.why: Scale and scope of operations exceed acceptable risk profile.

restrictions.rule: Applicants with more than $500,000 in contents must have a central alarm system.

restrictions.rule: Tenant exposures must be evaluated for general liability and pollution potential.
restrictions.why: Unassessed tenant operations may introduce unacceptable liability or environmental risk.

restrictions.rule: Fidelity coverage is prohibited.
restrictions.why: Employee dishonesty is outside the scope of covered exposures.

restrictions.rule: Professional liability coverage must be in effect for design or consulting services.
restrictions.why: Design errors and omissions are not covered under general liability.

restrictions.rule: Land, water, growing crops, or lawns are not covered property (except vegetated roofs).
restrictions.why: These exposures are uninsurable or outside standard property coverage.

restrictions.rule: Outdoor property such as fences must be specifically endorsed for coverage.
restrictions.why: Standard property forms may exclude certain outdoor items.

restrictions.rule: Services customary to medi-spas, schools, or tattoo parlors are ineligible.
restrictions.why: These services fall outside the intended scope of landscaping operations.

restrictions.rule: Drone photography or aerial surveying is not permitted.
restrictions.why: Aviation exposures are excluded from standard coverage.

Contractors who maintain Builders Risk and Inland Marine coverage for all projects and equipment (comprehensive protection).

Contractors with up to 30% of annual revenue from subcontracted work, provided all subcontractors are insured.
Businesses operating in suburban or rural areas with no work in major metropolitan centers.

Contractors who occasionally use rented equipment, provided Inland Marine coverage is maintained.

Contractors who perform seasonal work, with documented plans for managing off-season risks.
General contractors who do not perform work on buildings over three stories.
Contractors who do not engage in waterproofing, ship repair, or tree service/removal.
Businesses with a documented process for vetting and managing subcontractors.
Contractors who maintain Umbrella Liability coverage for excess protection.
not_acceptable: Contractors performing any work in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk, or Westchester counties (jurisdictional exclusion).
General contractors involved in heavy construction activities such as bridge construction, dredging, drilling, or tunneling (high hazard).
Contractors engaged in ship repair, marine construction, or waterproofing (excluded trades).
Businesses performing tree service, tree removal, or stump grinding (high risk of injury/property damage).
Roofing contractors or those performing any roofing work (elevated risk of falls and claims).
Excavation contractors or those performing any excavation or grading work (ground movement and collapse risk).
Handyperson businesses performing a wide range of unrelated trades (difficult to underwrite exposure).
Shop-only carpentry or sheet metal operations with no on-site construction (not within appetite).
Contractors with more than $1M in annual payroll or $2M in annual revenue (exceeds small business threshold).
Businesses with more than 30% of costs subcontracted (increased exposure to subcontractor risk).
Applicants seeking Hired and Non-Owned Auto Coverage (HNOA) (coverage not available).
Operations with multiple trades where any trade is ineligible (entire risk is ineligible).
Contractors with a history of regulatory violations or insurance claims in the past three years.
Contractors performing work on buildings over three stories in height.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for contractors performing work in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk, or Westchester counties.
restrictions.why: High litigation risk and unfavorable jurisdictional environment.

restrictions.rule: Heavy construction activities such as bridge construction, dredging, drilling, and tunneling are ineligible.
restrictions.why: These activities present elevated risk profiles outside underwriting appetite.

restrictions.rule: Contractors engaged in ship repair, marine construction, waterproofing, or tree service/removal are not eligible.

restrictions.rule: Roofers, handypersons, excavators, and tree removal/stump grinding services are ineligible.

restrictions.rule: Coverage eligibility is contingent on the nature of the work performed by the contractor.

Operations that perform scheduled, non-emergency work during standard business hours, reducing after-hours risk exposures.

Businesses that do not handle hazardous or specialty glass types (e.g., bulletproof, fire-rated) except as incidental work.

acceptable: Firms performing a mix of residential and light commercial glass work, provided high-rise or large-scale projects are not the primary focus.

Businesses that occasionally install specialty glass (e.g., tempered, laminated) with proper training and equipment.

Companies that perform storefront installations on single-story or low-rise commercial buildings.
Operations that adjust staffing seasonally to match demand, provided training and safety standards are maintained.
Businesses that use leased or rented vehicles for glass transport, provided insurance and safety standards are met.

Operations with a history of frequent or severe claims related to property damage, bodily injury, or auto accidents.
Businesses performing work on buildings above three stories or on high-rise structures.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for businesses primarily engaged in large-scale construction or high-rise glazing projects.
restrictions.why: These projects present high catastrophic loss exposure due to height, complexity, and potential for severe property damage or injury.

restrictions.rule: Businesses must have formal, written safety protocols and provide regular safety training to employees.
restrictions.why: Lack of safety measures increases the risk of workplace accidents and insurance claims.

restrictions.rule: Companies that subcontract most of their work must provide oversight and verify subcontractor insurance.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for operations working on buildings above three stories.

restrictions.rule: Agencies with inadequate financial stability or poor credit history may be subject to additional underwriting scrutiny or coverage restrictions.
restrictions.why: Financial instability increases the risk of business failure and unpaid claims.

restrictions.rule: Standard BOP coverage is not sufficient for agencies involved in property development or management; specialized coverage is required.
restrictions.why: These activities present unique risks not addressed by standard business owner policies.

business_types.name: Restaurants (Various Types: Full Service, Limited Service, Fast Food)

preferred: Quick-service or fast casual restaurants with tray or self-service models and no bar area, as these reduce liquor liability and slip-and-fall exposures.
Physical premises with a total floor area of 7,500 square feet or less, minimizing the risk of large-scale claims.
Seating capacity not exceeding 150 customers, which limits crowd-related hazards.
Alcohol sales limited to beer and wine only, with no liquor or spirits, reducing the potential for high-risk alcohol-related incidents.
Quick-service restaurants where alcohol sales do not exceed 25% of total sales, maintaining a manageable risk profile.
Full-service family restaurants where alcohol sales are limited to 30% of total revenue, ensuring food remains the primary focus.
No bar or cocktail lounge present on the premises, which lowers the risk of liquor liability.
Operations that maintain year-round business with no seasonal closures exceeding 30 consecutive days, ensuring consistent risk exposure.
Quick-service restaurants with limited cooking appliances and processes that produce grease-laden vapors, provided proper ventilation and fire suppression systems are in place.
Establishments with a diverse but moderate-sized staff, reducing the risk of employment-related claims.
Food service focused primarily on on-premises consumption, with food away from premises not exceeding 10% of total sales.
Vendors and suppliers are reputable and provide timely delivery of ingredients and supplies, supporting operational consistency.
Establishments with a manageable risk profile and no history of significant claims or regulatory violations.
Quick-service restaurants with no table service, which streamlines operations and reduces liability exposures.
Full-service family restaurants serving beer and wine only with meals, further limiting liquor liability.
acceptable: Full-service family restaurants with alcohol sales between 25% and 30% of total revenue, provided alcohol is limited to beer and wine served with meals.
Limited-service restaurants with minimal table service, provided no bar area is present and alcohol sales are within acceptable limits.
Quick-service restaurants with minor off-premises food sales, as long as it does not exceed 10% of total sales.
Restaurants with slightly higher seating capacity (up to 150) if all other risk factors are well controlled.
Establishments with minor seasonal fluctuations in business, provided there are no closures exceeding 30 consecutive days.
Quick-service restaurants utilizing limited cooking appliances that produce some grease-laden vapors, provided all fire safety measures are in place.
Operations with moderate alcohol service, provided strict adherence to regulatory requirements and staff training on responsible service.
Restaurants located in mixed-use developments, as long as they maintain a focus on food service and comply with all other guidelines.
Establishments combining light food preparation with ancillary services (such as catering), provided these services are minor and do not increase overall risk.
Restaurants with a history of minor claims, provided corrective actions have been implemented and risk management practices are in place.
Operations with moderate staff turnover, provided adequate training and supervision are maintained.
Restaurants with some delivery or takeout services, as long as these do not exceed 10% of total sales and proper food safety protocols are followed.
Full-service restaurants with a small, separate area for beer and wine storage, provided no bar or lounge is present.
Quick-service restaurants with extended hours, provided security and lighting are adequate.
Establishments with minor renovations or expansions, as long as they remain within the 7,500 sq ft and 150-seat limits.
not_acceptable: Restaurants with a bar or cocktail lounge, as these significantly increase liquor liability exposure.
Establishments where alcohol sales exceed 25% of total sales for quick-service or 30% for full-service family restaurants.
Operations selling liquor or spirits beyond beer and wine, due to higher risk of alcohol-related incidents.
Restaurants with a total floor area exceeding 7,500 square feet, increasing the potential for large-scale claims.
Seating capacity greater than 150 customers, which raises crowd management and safety concerns.
Seasonal operations that close for more than 30 consecutive days, leading to inconsistent risk exposure.
Quick-service restaurants offering table service, which is outside the preferred operational model.
Establishments where food away from the insured’s premises exceeds 10% of total sales, increasing delivery-related risks.
Restaurants with a history of significant claims, regulatory violations, or poor risk management practices.
Operations with high staff turnover and inadequate training, increasing the likelihood of employment-related claims.
Restaurants with inadequate fire suppression or ventilation systems in kitchens producing grease-laden vapors.
Establishments with a primary focus on alcohol sales rather than food service.
Quick-service restaurants with any bar area or lounge, regardless of alcohol sales percentage.
Operations with unlicensed or unregulated alcohol service, violating legal requirements.
Restaurants combining high-risk entertainment (such as live music or dancing) with food service, increasing liability exposures.

restrictions.rule: Alcohol sales must be limited to beer and wine only, with no liquor or spirits permitted.
restrictions.why: Liquor and spirits increase liquor liability exposure and are not within the preferred risk profile.

restrictions.rule: Alcohol sales in quick-service restaurants must not exceed 25% of total sales.
restrictions.why: Higher alcohol sales increase the risk of alcohol-related incidents and claims.

restrictions.rule: Alcohol sales in full-service family restaurants must not exceed 30% of total revenue.
restrictions.why: Maintaining a food-focused operation reduces liquor liability exposure.

restrictions.rule: No bar or cocktail lounge is permitted in quick-service restaurants.
restrictions.why: Bar areas significantly increase liquor liability and slip-and-fall risks.

restrictions.rule: Physical premises must not exceed 7,500 square feet in total floor area.
restrictions.why: Larger venues present greater risks for large-scale incidents and claims.

restrictions.rule: Seating capacity must not exceed 150 customers.
restrictions.why: Higher capacity increases crowd management and safety concerns.

restrictions.rule: No seasonal operations are allowed; establishments cannot be closed for more than 30 consecutive days.
restrictions.why: Seasonal closures lead to inconsistent risk exposure and complicate coverage.

restrictions.rule: Food away from the insured’s premises must not exceed 10% of total sales.
restrictions.why: Higher off-premises sales increase delivery and food safety risks.

restrictions.rule: Quick-service restaurants must not have any table service.
restrictions.why: Table service changes the operational model and increases liability exposures.

restrictions.rule: Establishments must maintain a focus on food service to qualify for coverage.
restrictions.why: Operations primarily focused on alcohol or ancillary services are outside the preferred risk appetite.

restrictions.rule: Quick-service restaurants must have a manageable risk profile and no history of significant claims.
restrictions.why: Past claims indicate higher ongoing risk and poor management practices.

restrictions.rule: All cooking appliances producing grease-laden vapors must have proper fire suppression and ventilation systems.
restrictions.why: Inadequate fire safety measures increase the risk of fire-related losses.

preferred: Facilities with secure, controlled access systems including electronic gate entry and 24/7 surveillance cameras, ensuring robust security for stored items.
Single-story or two-story self-storage facilities with enhanced fire suppression systems compliant with NFPA standards.
Facilities that maintain strict documentation of all portable storage unit contents on-site, supporting transparency and regulatory compliance.
Operations that prohibit storage of flammable, explosive, or toxic substances, reducing fire and contamination risks.
Facilities with on-site or contracted security personnel present during all hours of operation to deter theft and vandalism.
Self-storage businesses that offer climate-controlled units for sensitive items, provided all fire safety and building codes are met.
Facilities that sell packing supplies (boxes, tape, protective materials) as a secondary retail operation, supporting customer needs.
Facilities that maintain regular unit inspections and cleaning schedules, ensuring cleanliness and safety.
Operations that utilize online platforms for customer interaction, payments, and rental agreements, improving efficiency and recordkeeping.
Facilities that comply with all local zoning and building regulations, including restrictions on building height and materials stored.
Facilities that do not permit cold storage or storage of industrial materials, chemicals, pollutants, or waste.
Facilities that only allow limited quantities of household chemicals or small flammable liquids with proper endorsements and regulatory compliance.
Facilities that have established relationships with reputable security system providers and maintenance contractors.
Facilities that provide portable storage units on-site for less than or equal to 90 days, with full documentation and adherence to fire safety protocols.
Facilities that maintain continuous (24/7) surveillance system operation, ensuring ongoing monitoring of premises.
acceptable: Facilities with portable storage units on-site for more than 90 days, provided specialized endorsements and risk mitigation measures are in place.
Multi-story (up to two stories) self-storage facilities with enhanced fire suppression systems and full compliance with local building codes.
Facilities that allow limited quantities of hazardous materials (such as household chemicals) with proper documentation, endorsements, and adherence to all regulations.
Facilities that contract out security personnel rather than employing them directly, as long as security coverage is continuous.
Facilities that experience seasonal fluctuations in occupancy and implement promotional offers during off-peak times to maintain business.
Facilities that provide storage solutions for contractors and small businesses, provided all storage is non-hazardous and compliant with regulations.
Facilities that utilize electronic access systems for customer entry and exit, with regular audits of access logs.
Facilities that maintain a retail area for packing supplies as a minor portion of their business operations.
Facilities that use portable storage units for temporary overflow, with strict adherence to fire safety and documentation protocols.
Facilities that maintain compliance with NFPA Standard #96 for any applicable operations.
Facilities that employ maintenance staff for routine repairs and cleaning, ensuring operational efficiency.
Facilities that maintain up-to-date records of customer contracts and storage unit assignments.
Facilities that have implemented risk mitigation measures for extended portable storage unit use.
Facilities that do not exceed two stories in height, with no limitation on floor area.
Facilities that provide storage for students, residential customers, and small businesses, excluding prohibited materials.
not_acceptable: Facilities that permit storage of flammable, explosive, or toxic substances without proper endorsements or in violation of regulations.
Facilities that allow cold storage or storage of industrial materials, chemicals, pollutants, or waste.
Facilities that exceed two stories in height, regardless of fire suppression systems.
Facilities that lack controlled access systems or do not operate surveillance cameras continuously (24/7).
Facilities that do not maintain documentation of portable storage unit contents on-site.
Facilities that allow portable storage units to remain on-site for more than 90 days without specialized endorsements and risk mitigation.
Facilities that do not comply with local building codes or zoning regulations.
Facilities that do not have enhanced fire suppression systems in multi-story buildings.
Facilities that lack on-site or contracted security personnel for secure premises.
Facilities that permit dancing, live entertainment, or any activities beyond incidental music.
Facilities that do not comply with NFPA Standard #96 where applicable.
Facilities that do not adhere to fire safety protocols for portable storage units.
Facilities that allow storage of hazardous materials without proper endorsements and regulatory compliance.
Facilities that do not maintain regular unit inspections or cleaning schedules.
Facilities that do not comply with all regulatory requirements for storage practices.

restrictions.rule: No storage of flammable, explosive, or toxic substances without proper endorsements.
restrictions.why: Reduces risk of fire, explosion, and environmental contamination.

restrictions.rule: Self-storage facilities must not exceed two stories in height.
restrictions.why: Limits fire and life safety risks in multi-story buildings.

restrictions.rule: Portable storage units allowed on-site for 90 days or less with documentation and fire safety compliance.
restrictions.why: Limits risk associated with temporary storage and ensures regulatory oversight.

restrictions.rule: Portable storage units on-site for more than 90 days require specialized endorsements and risk mitigation.
restrictions.why: Extended use increases risk and requires additional controls.

restrictions.rule: No cold storage or storage of industrial materials, chemicals, pollutants, or waste is permitted.
restrictions.why: Prevents high-risk and ineligible storage types.

restrictions.rule: Continuous (24/7) surveillance systems and controlled access must be maintained.
restrictions.why: Ensures ongoing security and monitoring of premises.

restrictions.rule: On-site or contracted security personnel are required for secure premises.
restrictions.why: Deters theft, vandalism, and unauthorized access.

restrictions.rule: Enhanced fire suppression systems are mandatory for multi-story facilities.
restrictions.why: Mitigates fire risk in larger buildings.

restrictions.rule: Strict adherence to fire safety protocols for all portable storage units.
restrictions.why: Reduces risk of fire and ensures compliance with regulations.

restrictions.rule: Documentation of contents is required for all portable storage units on-site.
restrictions.why: Supports transparency and regulatory compliance.

restrictions.rule: No dancing or live entertainment (other than incidental music) is permitted.
restrictions.why: Limits liability and maintains business eligibility.

restrictions.rule: Compliance with local building codes and NFPA standards is required.
restrictions.why: Ensures legal operation and safety of the facility.

preferred: Businesses with stable and verifiable financial statements demonstrating consistent revenue and expense management.
Fixed-location shoe stores with well-maintained, clean, and organized premises that meet or exceed local safety codes.
Shoe repair shops employing skilled technicians or cobblers with documented training and experience.
Operations with a documented strong safety record, showing minimal or no slip-and-fall incidents or workplace injuries over the past three years.
Retailers and repair shops that do not engage in equipment rental or leasing as part of their business model.
Mobile shoe repair services operating exclusively with properly insured commercial vehicles and drivers with clean driving records.
Businesses that maintain up-to-date inventory management systems and regularly review stock to match seasonal demand.
Operations that have implemented corrective measures following any moderate claims history, with evidence of improved safety protocols.
Shoe stores and repair shops sourcing inventory and materials from reputable, established vendors or suppliers.
Businesses with clear, documented policies for customer service, returns, and complaint resolution.
Retailers and repair shops that actively participate in local advertising, social media, or community events to attract and retain customers.
Mobile repair services that comply with all geographic service area restrictions and local licensing requirements.
Shoe repair operations using only non-hazardous materials and standard, low-risk equipment for repairs.
Businesses with regular staff safety training and compliance checks documented annually.
Operations with no history of regulatory violations, fines, or unresolved safety code infractions.
acceptable: Shoe stores or repair shops with moderate claims history, provided that documented corrective actions have been taken.
Mobile shoe repair services with minor past insurance lapses, now fully compliant and properly insured.
Businesses with minor, resolved safety code violations and evidence of ongoing compliance.
Retailers with older premises that have undergone recent renovations to address safety and accessibility.
Operations with limited marketing or community engagement but strong customer retention and satisfaction metrics.
Repair shops using basic adhesives and materials, provided all substances are stored and handled according to safety guidelines.
Businesses with part-time or seasonal staff, provided all employees receive adequate safety and operational training.
Retailers or repair shops with a small number of customer complaints, all of which have been resolved satisfactorily.
Mobile services operating in multiple jurisdictions, provided all necessary permits and insurance are in place.
Shoe stores with limited display space but effective inventory management and customer service practices.
Repair shops with a single skilled technician, provided there is a documented backup plan for coverage during absences.
Businesses sourcing materials from a mix of local and national suppliers, with no supply chain disruptions in the past year.
Operations with minor, non-recurring workplace injuries that have resulted in updated safety protocols.
Retailers or repair shops with moderate seasonal fluctuations in revenue, but stable year-over-year financials.
Businesses with a recent change in ownership, provided there is continuity in safety and operational procedures.
not_acceptable: Businesses engaged in equipment rental or leasing as a primary or secondary business activity.
Shoe repair operations using hazardous chemicals, solvents, or high-risk machinery not suitable for small-scale operations.
Mobile repair services operating without proper commercial vehicle insurance or with a history of uninsured incidents.
Retailers or repair shops with unresolved or repeated safety code violations or regulatory fines.
Businesses with a history of frequent slip-and-fall incidents or workplace injuries without evidence of corrective action.
Operations with unverified or incomplete financial records, or evidence of financial instability.
Shoe stores or repair shops located in premises with significant structural issues or ongoing maintenance problems.
Mobile services operating outside of permitted geographic service areas or without required local licenses.
Businesses with ongoing or unresolved customer complaints related to safety, service, or product quality.
Repair shops using industrial-grade equipment or materials classified as hazardous by local or federal regulations.
Retailers or repair shops with a pattern of insurance claims indicating poor risk management or unsafe practices.
Operations with no documented staff training or safety protocols in place.
Businesses with a history of supply chain disruptions leading to frequent inventory shortages or customer dissatisfaction.
Shoe stores or repair shops sharing premises with unrelated high-risk businesses (e.g., auto repair, chemical processing).
Operations that have been subject to regulatory shutdowns, license revocations, or legal actions related to safety or compliance.

restrictions.rule: No businesses engaged in equipment rental or leasing are permitted.
restrictions.why: Equipment rental or leasing introduces additional liability and operational risks outside the scope of standard shoe retail or repair.

restrictions.rule: All fixed-location premises must be well-maintained and compliant with local safety codes.
restrictions.why: Poorly maintained premises increase the risk of accidents and regulatory violations.

restrictions.rule: Mobile shoe repair services must operate only with properly insured commercial vehicles.
restrictions.why: Uninsured vehicles present significant liability exposure in the event of accidents or claims.

restrictions.rule: Mobile services must comply with all geographic service area restrictions and local licensing requirements.
restrictions.why: Operating outside permitted areas or without proper licenses can result in legal and regulatory penalties.

restrictions.rule: Small-scale shoe repair operations must not use hazardous materials or high-risk equipment.
restrictions.why: Hazardous materials and high-risk equipment elevate the potential for workplace injuries and environmental hazards.

restrictions.rule: Businesses must maintain a documented strong safety record with minimal or no slip-and-fall incidents or workplace injuries.
restrictions.why: A poor safety record indicates inadequate risk management and increases the likelihood of future claims.

restrictions.rule: Moderate claims history is only acceptable if corrective measures have been implemented and documented.
restrictions.why: Corrective actions demonstrate a commitment to improving safety and reducing future risk.

restrictions.rule: All staff must receive regular safety and operational training, with records maintained annually.
restrictions.why: Ongoing training reduces the risk of accidents and ensures compliance with best practices.

restrictions.rule: Businesses must have verifiable financials and demonstrate financial stability.
restrictions.why: Financial instability increases the risk of business failure and associated insurance claims.

restrictions.rule: No unresolved or repeated regulatory violations or safety code infractions are permitted.
restrictions.why: Ongoing non-compliance indicates systemic issues and heightened risk exposure.

preferred: Properties with a tenant mix consisting primarily of low-risk businesses such as professional offices, boutique retail stores, and service-oriented businesses, as these tenants present lower liability and property risk.
Shopping centers anchored by pharmacies, coffee shops, or small accounting firms, which typically generate steady foot traffic and have a stable business model.
Buildings with up-to-date fire suppression systems, including sprinklers and fire alarms, to mitigate fire risk.
Properties with comprehensive security measures, such as security cameras, alarm systems, and adequate exterior and interior lighting, to deter crime and vandalism.
Centers with a clean claims history, showing no or minimal prior losses, indicating effective risk management and maintenance practices.
Properties located in areas with low crime rates, reducing the likelihood of theft, vandalism, and liability claims.
Well-maintained buildings with regular maintenance schedules and documented repairs, ensuring property condition is consistently high.
Properties with adequate and well-marked parking facilities, minimizing slip-and-fall exposures and improving customer safety.
Centers that comply fully with all local safety regulations and building codes, including ADA accessibility requirements.
Properties with stable, long-term tenants under clear lease agreements, reducing turnover and vacancy risk.
Shopping centers that have undergone recent renovations or upgrades to address aging infrastructure and improve safety features.
Properties with no history of environmental hazards or contamination, reducing potential liability and cleanup costs.
Centers with amenities such as parks or playgrounds that are well-maintained and regularly inspected for safety.
Properties with effective tenant screening and lease management processes in place, ensuring a consistent risk profile.
Centers located in economically stable areas with strong consumer demand, supporting tenant viability and occupancy rates.
acceptable: Properties with a broader tenant mix, including some moderate-risk businesses such as small restaurants or fitness studios, provided overall risk remains reasonable.
Centers with minor prior claims that have been fully remediated and have implemented corrective actions to prevent recurrence.
Buildings with older safety systems that are functional but scheduled for upgrades within a defined timeframe.
Properties located in areas with moderate crime rates but with enhanced security measures in place.
Centers with a mix of short-term and long-term tenants, provided vacancy rates are low and lease terms are stable.
Properties with minor deferred maintenance issues that are documented and scheduled for repair.
Centers with public parking availability that meets local standards, even if not exclusively dedicated to the property.
Properties with some exposure to environmental hazards that have been assessed and mitigated according to regulatory requirements.
Centers with amenities such as playgrounds or parks that have documented safety inspections and maintenance logs.
Properties with a limited history of slip-and-fall claims, provided risk mitigation measures have been implemented.
Centers in areas experiencing moderate economic fluctuation but with a history of stable occupancy.
Properties with tenants in higher-risk categories (e.g., small restaurants) that have strong safety protocols and loss control measures.
Centers with older buildings that have been partially renovated to address key safety and structural concerns.
Properties that are in compliance with most, but not all, local codes, with a documented plan to achieve full compliance.
Centers with a history of minor vandalism incidents that have been addressed through improved security.
not_acceptable: Properties with a tenant mix dominated by high-risk businesses such as nightclubs, bars, cannabis dispensaries, or adult entertainment venues, due to elevated liability and property risks.
Centers with a history of frequent or severe claims, including multiple slip-and-fall incidents, fires, or vandalism, indicating poor risk management.
Buildings with outdated or non-functional fire suppression and alarm systems, increasing the risk of catastrophic loss.
Properties located in high-crime areas without adequate security measures, significantly raising the risk of theft and liability claims.
Centers with significant deferred maintenance, structural deficiencies, or code violations that have not been addressed.
Properties with known environmental contamination or unresolved hazardous material issues, posing substantial liability exposure.
Centers with inadequate or poorly maintained parking facilities, leading to increased risk of accidents and liability claims.
Properties with a high percentage of vacant units or unstable tenant base, increasing the risk of property deterioration and loss of income.
Centers that do not comply with local safety regulations, building codes, or ADA requirements, exposing owners to regulatory penalties.
Properties with amenities such as playgrounds or parks that lack regular safety inspections or have a history of injury claims.
Centers in economically distressed areas with high vacancy rates and declining tenant demand.
Properties with tenants engaged in illegal or unlicensed activities, creating significant legal and reputational risks.
Centers with repeated claims related to water damage, mold, or other maintenance-related issues that have not been properly remediated.
Properties with no documented maintenance or risk management procedures, indicating a lack of proactive loss control.
Centers with significant exposure to natural disaster risks (e.g., flood zones, wildfire areas) without appropriate mitigation measures in place.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with a majority of high-risk tenants such as nightclubs, bars, cannabis dispensaries, or adult entertainment venues.
restrictions.why: These tenants significantly increase liability and property risk, leading to higher frequency and severity of claims.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with unresolved code violations or non-compliance with local safety regulations.
restrictions.why: Non-compliance exposes the property to regulatory action and increases the risk of loss.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with a history of frequent or severe claims, including multiple slip-and-fall, fire, or vandalism incidents.
restrictions.why: A poor claims history indicates ineffective risk management and higher future loss potential.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with significant deferred maintenance or structural deficiencies.
restrictions.why: Deferred maintenance increases the likelihood of property damage and liability claims.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with known environmental contamination or unresolved hazardous material issues.
restrictions.why: Environmental hazards pose substantial liability and cleanup costs.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties located in high-crime areas without adequate security measures in place.
restrictions.why: High-crime locations increase the risk of theft, vandalism, and liability claims.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with inadequate or poorly maintained parking facilities.
restrictions.why: Poor parking conditions increase the risk of accidents and liability exposures.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with a high percentage of vacant units or unstable tenant base.
restrictions.why: High vacancy increases the risk of property deterioration and loss of rental income.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with amenities such as playgrounds or parks that lack regular safety inspections.
restrictions.why: Uninspected amenities increase the risk of injury claims and liability.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with tenants engaged in illegal or unlicensed activities.
restrictions.why: Illegal activities create significant legal, regulatory, and reputational risks.

restrictions.rule: Do not accept properties with repeated claims related to water damage, mold, or maintenance issues that have not been remediated.
restrictions.why: Unresolved maintenance issues indicate ongoing risk and potential for future claims.

preferred: Stores with no sales, rental, or repair of firearms or ammunition; reduces exposure to high-severity liability claims.
Retailers specializing in non-motorized sporting goods such as apparel, footwear, and general fitness equipment; lower product liability risk.
Stores with a documented history of risk management practices and no significant claims in the past five years; demonstrates strong operational controls.
Locations with robust safety protocols and staff certifications for all instructional activities; mitigates injury risk.
Stores that maintain up-to-date documentation of product safety recalls and compliance with manufacturer guidelines; reduces recall-related liability.
Retailers with less than 10% of annual receipts from rental operations and comprehensive rental agreements; limits exposure from equipment misuse.
Stores that do not offer high-risk sports equipment such as climbing gear, scuba equipment, or motorized vehicles; lowers underwriting risk.
Businesses with established vendor relationships and documented supply chain quality controls; ensures product reliability.
Stores that conduct regular employee training on customer safety and product use; minimizes injury claims.
Retailers located in commercial districts with adequate security and loss prevention measures; reduces theft and premises liability.
Stores with seasonal staffing adjustments and documented onboarding/training for temporary staff; maintains consistent safety standards.
Retailers that do not offer on-site repair or modification of sporting equipment; avoids liability from improper repairs.
Stores with less than 5% of annual receipts from gun or ammunition sales, with no repair or rental; aligns with underwriting guidelines.
Retailers that provide clear customer instructions and signage for safe equipment use; supports risk mitigation.
Stores with a proactive approach to regulatory compliance and regular internal audits; ensures adherence to local laws.
acceptable: Stores with limited sales (less than 5% of receipts) of firearms or ammunition, with no repair or rental; exposure is controlled.
Retailers offering instructional services for low- to moderate-risk sports (e.g., tennis, golf, running) with certified staff; manageable injury risk.
Stores with seasonal rental operations for non-motorized equipment, provided maintenance logs are kept; risk is monitored.
Retailers selling a moderate volume of high-risk sports equipment (e.g., archery, cycling) with documented safety protocols; risk controls in place.
Stores with a minor history of claims, provided corrective actions and improved risk management are demonstrated; risk is improving.
Retailers with a mix of general sporting goods and niche products, provided high-risk items are a small portion of sales; exposure is diversified.
Stores that participate in manufacturer recall programs and promptly remove affected products; liability is managed.
Retailers with instructional activities requiring waivers and participant acknowledgment of risks; legal exposure is reduced.
Stores that provide equipment rental with customer orientation and signed agreements; risk is addressed.
Retailers located in shopping malls or commercial centers with shared security; premises risk is moderate.
Stores with a mix of permanent and temporary staff, provided all receive safety training; maintains operational standards.
Retailers with some high-value inventory, provided theft prevention measures are in place; property risk is controlled.
Stores with a moderate volume of product sales from reputable brands; supply chain risk is acceptable.
Retailers that sell or rent motorized sporting equipment but have specialized coverage and risk controls; higher risk but manageable.
Stores with a history of minor regulatory violations, provided corrective actions have been implemented; compliance is improving.
not_acceptable: Stores with more than 5% of annual receipts from gun or ammunition sales, or any repair or rental of firearms; exceeds underwriting guidelines.
Retailers offering repair or modification services for firearms, ammunition, or high-risk motorized equipment; unacceptable liability exposure.
Stores with significant sales or rentals of motorized sporting equipment (e.g., ATVs, jet skis) without specialized risk controls; high injury risk.
Retailers with a history of frequent or severe liability claims related to product defects or customer injuries; unacceptable claims experience.
Stores lacking documented safety protocols or staff certifications for instructional activities; insufficient risk management.
Retailers that do not comply with local, state, or federal safety and liability regulations; regulatory risk is too high.
Stores with a high volume of high-risk sports equipment sales (e.g., climbing, scuba, skydiving) without adequate risk controls; exposure is excessive.
Retailers with ongoing or unresolved product recall issues; liability risk is unmanageable.
Stores that allow unsupervised use of rental equipment or lack customer orientation; increases injury risk.
Retailers with no documented employee training on safety or product use; operational risk is unacceptable.
Stores with a pattern of failing to respond to manufacturer safety bulletins or recalls; product liability is elevated.
Retailers with inadequate or missing documentation of risk management practices; cannot verify controls.
Stores that routinely modify or alter sporting equipment for customers; increases product liability.
Retailers with a history of regulatory enforcement actions or fines for safety violations; compliance risk is too high.
Stores with significant claims related to instructional activities and no corrective action taken; ongoing exposure.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for stores with more than 5% of annual receipts from gun or ammunition sales.
restrictions.why: High-severity liability exposure from firearms exceeds underwriting appetite.

restrictions.rule: No coverage for any repair or rental of firearms or ammunition.
restrictions.why: Repair and rental activities introduce unacceptable product liability and injury risks.

restrictions.rule: Specialized coverage and risk controls required for stores selling or renting motorized sporting equipment.
restrictions.why: Motorized equipment presents elevated injury and product liability risks.

restrictions.rule: All instructional activities must be conducted by certified staff with documented safety protocols.
restrictions.why: Proper training and protocols are essential to mitigate injury claims.

restrictions.rule: Stores must maintain documentation of safety protocols, staff certifications, and product recalls.
restrictions.why: Documentation is necessary for underwriting and claims defense.

restrictions.rule: Rental operations require signed customer agreements and equipment maintenance logs.
restrictions.why: Reduces liability from misuse or malfunction of rented equipment.

restrictions.rule: Coverage may be limited or excluded for stores with a history of frequent or severe claims.
restrictions.why: Past claims indicate ongoing or unaddressed risk exposures.

restrictions.rule: Stores must comply with all local, state, and federal safety and liability regulations.
restrictions.why: Regulatory compliance is critical to avoid fines and liability claims.

restrictions.rule: Additional underwriting information required for stores with high-risk product sales or instructional services.
restrictions.why: Detailed risk assessment is needed for higher-exposure operations.

restrictions.rule: Liability coverage limits may be adjusted based on the nature and volume of products sold.
restrictions.why: Higher-risk products require higher limits or additional exclusions.

restrictions.rule: Stores must implement customer safety measures, including signage and instructions for equipment use.
restrictions.why: Proactive safety measures help reduce the likelihood of injury claims.

preferred: Retail stationery stores operating from a single physical location with standard business hours (lower risk profile, easier to monitor).
Businesses with robust inventory management systems and regular stock audits (reduces risk of loss or mismanagement).
Operations that source products from established, reputable suppliers with documented quality controls (minimizes product liability exposure).
Businesses that implement clear labeling and safety information on all products, especially those intended for children (compliance with regulatory standards).
